claim: Berenson and others 1995 (definitions, no measurement): lost update (phenomenon P4) is possible at READ COMMITTED, and snapshot isolation's first-committer-wins rule prevents it.

Berenson and others 1995: under dirty write two writers' uncommitted changes to two related items both survive and break the constraint between them (x = y ends as x=2, y=1), and undoing one writer by restoring its before-image would wipe out the other's update.

Berenson and others 1995: read skew (A5A) and write skew (A5B) are separate anomalies, and snapshot isolation allows write skew: two writers that each read a consistent pair and write different items can break a constraint between the items.

Berenson and others 1995: snapshot isolation does not preclude phantoms (P3): with a constraint that the hours of a set of tasks chosen by a predicate cannot sum above 8, two concurrent transactions that each read the predicate and insert a different task are not stopped by first-committer-wins.

Ports and Grittner 2012 (PostgreSQL's serializable snapshot isolation): on DBT-2++ and RUBiS serializable mode cost less than 7 % of throughput against snapshot isolation (5 % in the CPU-bound in-memory run), on the disk-bound run it was indistinguishable from SI with serialization failures under 0.25 %, and on the SIBENCH microbenchmark read tracking cost 10-20 % CPU; the low cost came from dangerous structures being rare, not from low contention, since RUBiS contains frequent rw-conflicts.
note: The draft said 'low contention' and '4 to 36 client threads'; the refuter found the first contradicted and the second not in the text.

claim: Ports and Grittner 2012: in PostgreSQL's SSI, long-running read-only transactions that access large amounts of data take more SIREAD locks and are more likely to conflict, and while they run they hold back the cleanup of other transactions' SIREAD locks; deferrable transactions that wait for a safe snapshot avoid both.
note: The extra locks come from the data read, not from the length; only the cleanup effect is due to length (refuter).

claim: Ports and Grittner 2012: SSI's check may have false positives, because not every dangerous structure is part of a cycle; PostgreSQL reduces them with its read-only optimisation but keeps them.

PostgreSQL documentation (Transaction Isolation) and Ports and Grittner 2012: on a serialization failure the application should abort the current transaction and retry the whole transaction from the beginning; the second time through, the transaction sees the previously committed change as part of its initial view, and users must already be prepared to handle transactions aborted by serialization failures.
note: Reasoned (refuter): the documented retry runs the same program on new data and may act differently; what does not carry to sessions is its cost and a program that may be wrong differently on each run. The quoted error at page.txt 145-146 is Repeatable Read's.

claim: Gray, Lorie, Putzolu and Traiger 1976 (protocol and argument, no measurement): the choice of lockable unit trades concurrency against overhead; a writer of a small unit first tags every ancestor with an intention mode, and intention mode is compatible with itself.

InnoDB manual (documentation, rules, no measurement): InnoDB supports multiple granularity locking, so row locks and table locks coexist, and its intention locks do not block anything except full table requests.

InnoDB manual: gap locks are purely inhibitive (they only stop others inserting into the gap) and do not conflict with each other, and insert-intention locks let transactions inserting into the same gap at different positions proceed without waiting for each other.

Eswaran, Gray, Lorie and Traiger 1976: deciding whether two general predicates conflict is recursively unsolvable, so it is not clear how to make predicate locks work, and the paper restricts them to simple predicates.

Graefe 2010 (survey of B-tree locking; designs, no measurement): key-range locking, a special form of predicate locking whose predicates are intervals of the index's sort order, is what products use, while neither pure predicate locking nor precision locking has been adopted in major products; deleting a key requires a lock on both the old key and its neighbour; a fine granularity of locking is required most often at hot spots.

Ries and Stonebraker 1977 (simulation, OCR table; 10 transactions over 5,000 entities, each touching 50 to 500): useful I/O was 7041.957 with 1 granule, 9437.987 with 10 and 9572.718 with 20, near the peak, and fell steeply beyond a few hundred granules; the authors concluded that in most cases 10 granules appear sufficient. The value at 1,000 granules cannot be fixed from the OCR table.
note: The draft's 34 % and 64 % were computed from the rows; the 64 % rested on a row that may belong to 750 or 1,000 granules.

claim: Ries and Stonebraker 1977 (simulation): the number of entities a transaction touches had the most effect on the desired number of granules, which rose as transactions got smaller; even for transactions touching a very small part of the database a large number of granules interfered with throughput, and keeping locks in main memory appeared to make little difference.

Srinivasan and Carey 1993 (simulation; 1 CPU, 8 disks, a buffer pool of 200; a tree of 40,000 entries and around 250 leaf pages): with locks held to the end of the transaction there was virtually no difference between leaf-page and record locking at 1 operation per transaction, while at 10 operations leaf-page locking performed much worse, a severe loss of throughput from deadlocks, aborts and re-execution; the size of the loss is in a figure not read as text.

SQL Server documentation (Lock Escalation): escalation converts many fine-grain locks into fewer coarse-grain locks, reducing system overhead while increasing the probability of contention; it is triggered when one Transact-SQL statement acquires at least 5,000 locks on a single reference of a table or index, or when lock memory reaches a threshold (24 percent of the engine's memory at the default setting), and a blocked escalation is retried at every 1,250 new locks.

Graefe 2007 (an argument with an example, no measurement): a single ill-advised lock escalation suffices to collapse the multi-programming level to one, and SQL Server does not support lock de-escalation.

Kung and Robinson 1981 (as quoted in the earlier round's reading): optimistic methods may well be superior to locking where transaction conflict is highly unlikely; their major difficulty is starvation, and their cure restarts the starving transaction without releasing the critical section, which is equivalent to write-locking the entire database.

Larson and others 2012 (main-memory engine; long readers each scan 10 percent of a 10M-row table): with only short update transactions the single-version engine was twice as fast as the multiversion schemes; one long reader cut its update throughput 75% against 5% for multiversion, and with 50% of the active transactions long readers multiversion had 80X its update throughput.

Silo, Tu and others 2013 (as quoted in the earlier round's reading; TPC-C with one hot counter per district): read-write conflicts on the counter raise aborts under OCC, and under 2PL conflicting workers would serialize around its write locks; against the partition-locked store Silo was up to 8.20x faster at 24 workers with the counter and 17.21x at 32 workers with the counter taken out of the transaction; the gain from taking the counter out within Silo is not stated.

Silo, Tu and others 2013: Silo assumes a one-shot request model, and the authors state that if high-latency client communication were part of a transaction the likelihood of abort due to concurrent updates would grow (stated, not measured).

Silo, Tu and others 2013: a store partitioned by owner beat Silo's OCC by 1.54x with no cross-partition transactions, fell below it at roughly 20% cross-partition transactions, and lost by 2.98x at roughly 60%.

Yu and others 2014 (simulation to 1,024 cores): a 2PL engine with a fixed lock order scaled almost linearly with no skew and peaked at 16 cores at theta 0.8; in a separate skew sweep at 64 cores every scheme dropped sharply above theta 0.6 and approached zero above 0.8; at theta 0.8 on 1024 cores OCC did best because one transaction is always allowed to commit.

Harding and others 2017 (16 servers, YCSB): the protocols' throughput was little affected by skew up to theta 0.5, and once theta reached 0.8 all but one converged to the same low performance; Calvin alone kept good performance.

TicToc, Yu and others 2016 (in memory, a 40-core machine with 80 threads): up to 92% better throughput than four earlier schemes (two 2PL variants, Hekaton, Silo) in the best case of the sweeps; its data-driven commit order alone gave 35.6% over Silo on TPC-C with 4 warehouses and 10% on high-contention YCSB, most of the high-contention gain came from no-wait locking and pre-emptive aborts; at high write contention it did not reduce aborts, and its advantage over Silo disappeared at 80 warehouses.

Cicada, Lim and others 2017 (one 28-core machine): inexpensive aborts can make high abort rates acceptable, and aborts can be expensive (CPU cycles and cache-line invalidation, worse when retried too fast).

Tanabe and others 2020 (CCBench, in memory, 224 threads on 224 cores): in 2PL, Wait began to outperform NoWait as the number of operations per transaction increased, which the authors explain by abort-retry cost rising with length; in Silo, NoWait outperformed Wait; their insight is that one cannot give a general statement about which is better.

FoundationDB, Zhou and others 2021 (the engine's own paper): its OCC design avoids the logic of acquiring and releasing locks, and works well because the transaction conflict rate is very low, less than 1% (self-reported, multi-tenant production); it keeps a 5-second MVCC window and says many transactions that may span more than 5s can be divided into smaller transactions.

Agrawal, Carey and Livny 1987 (simulation, as quoted in the earlier round's reading): dynamic two-phase locking beat immediate restart and optimistic control at medium to high resource utilisation; a restart-oriented algorithm was better only when utilisation was low enough to tolerate much wasted work and, in addition, a large number of transactions were available to execute (many resource units, or interactive think times of 1, 5 or 10 s); the authors call it an open question whether such low utilisations occur in real systems.

Hekaton, Diaconu and others 2013: a transaction that begins while another is in its validation phase becomes dependent on it if it reads a version the other created or ignores one it deleted; rather than block, it takes a commit dependency and may commit only if the other commits, so if the other aborts it must also abort and cascading aborts are possible.

Calvin, Thomson and others 2012: deterministic locking requires advance knowledge of all transactions' read and write sets before execution; a transaction that must read to learn them runs a reconnaissance pass and is restarted if the sets changed.

Abadi and Faleiro 2018 (survey of deterministic databases): if transactions do not know their access sets in advance they must run approximately serially, and for interactive transactions either the client declares the access set or the system defaults to slow serial execution.
Abadi and Faleiro 2018 (survey): requesting and granting locks in the order transactions appear in the input log is deadlock-free, and it needs each transaction's access set before it runs.
note: The draft cited line 35, a requirement on deterministic systems; the ordered-locking statement is line 52 (refuter).

claim: Aria, Lu and others 2020 (one node, 12 worker threads, YCSB): at low contention (abort rate about 0.4 %) Aria had 2.4x the throughput of Calvin and 10.3x that of PB, a replicated primary-backup engine with strict 2PL; at skew 0.999 it kept only 39% of its throughput without skew because aborted transactions rerun, and above skew 0.8 and 0.9 it was below PWV and BOHM.

Doppel, Narula and others 2014 (20 cores, in memory): when 100% of transactions increment one hot key, splitting it per core and applying the commuting updates separately gave 38x OCC, 19x 2PL and 6.2x Atomic; it needs the contended updates to be commutative, else it runs the transactions serially; transactions that read split data wait for the next joined phase (higher latency); a larger application gained 3x.
Doppel, Narula and others 2014: the system cannot leave a joined phase until all current transactions commit or abort.

Clements and others 2013 (scalable commutativity rule, an operating-system result): in any situation where interface operations commute they have an implementation whose memory accesses are conflict-free in that situation, no single implementation need be conflict-free in all of them, and commutativity suffices but may not be necessary; an interface can be changed to commute, as an open that must allocate the lowest unused file descriptor does not.

Bailis and others 2014 (invariant confluence, as quoted in the earlier round's reading): operations that keep an invariant under merge need no coordination, giving over 12.7M TPC-C New-Order transactions per second on 200 servers, a 25-fold improvement over prior results; order IDs assigned sequentially per district do need coordination; if invariants are incorrectly or incompletely specified, correctness may be violated.

O'Neil 1986 (escrow, a method; the paper measures nothing): a quantity updated with great frequency is a hot spot, so access to it must be permitted without excluding other transactions except for the shortest possible time; holding a lock on a quantity for the length of a transaction, even one that lasts just a second or so, is unacceptable.

Yu and others 2014 (simulation, uniform access) and Harding and others 2017 (16 servers), as quoted in the earlier round's reading: H-Store outperformed all other schemes up to 800 cores on single-partition work and did not scale once transactions touched four or more partitions; separately, every protocol but Calvin lost 12-40% from two to four partitions per transaction, a cost of distribution, not of ownership.

Jepsen's analysis of VoltDB 6.3 (Kingsbury 2016, funded by VoltDB): VoltDB's internal benchmarks suggest multi-partition transactions are practically limited to a few hundred updates per second (the vendor's figure, self-reported).

Apel and others 2011 (semistructured merge, 180 Java merge scenarios, as quoted in the earlier round's reading): it reduced conflicts in 60 % of scenarios by 34±21 % and increased them in 26 % (46 of 180) by 109±170 %; renaming is a challenge because it relies on nominal equality.

Cavalcanti, Borba and Accioly 2017 (34,030 scenarios from 50 Java projects, as quoted in the earlier round's reading): semistructured merge reported 14,544 conflicts against 19,238 for line merge, about 24% fewer; its estimated additional false negatives (wrong clean merges) were 20.60 ± 21.30 % against 9.62 ± 16.29 % for line merge (overestimated upper bounds), and the authors find no evidence of fewer false negatives; their improved tool s3m halved reported conflicts with at least 8% fewer false negatives.

Apel, Lessenich and Lengauer 2012 (JDime, 8 Java projects, 72 scenarios, as quoted in the earlier round's reading): full structured merge reported 39 % of the conflicts of line merge, and trying line merge first and switching to tree merge only where it conflicts was up to 12 times faster than pure tree merge, 5 times on average.

Larsen and others 2022 (Spork, structured merge for Java): Spork ignores delete/edit conflicts, where one revision deletes a subtree in which the other edits; in 3DM-Merge such a deletion silently overrides the edits.

Ellis, Nadi and Dig 2022 (preprint; 2,001 merge scenarios chosen for refactoring conflicts in 20 Java projects): RefMerge resolved or reduced conflicts in 497 (25%) scenarios while increasing conflicting lines in 214 (11%); IntelliMerge resolved or reduced them in 478 (24%) but increased conflicting lines in 597 (30%).

Sousa, Dillig and Lahiri 2018 (SafeMerge, Java, one method at a time, a filtered set): of 52 non-trivial real merges, kdiff3 produced five textual merges that SafeMerge judged semantically incorrect, three after removing two of the verifier's false positives; verification took an average of 0.5 second per benchmark.
Da Silva and others 2023 (SAM, preprint; Java, generated unit tests per change): the best configuration detected nine of 28 known semantic conflicts.

Xu, Subramanian and Karthik 2026 (preprint; pull requests of AI coding agents on GitHub): co-active pairs had textual conflicts in 19.8% of 601 evaluatable same-agent pairs and 41.7% of 115 evaluatable cross-agent pairs; build and semantic conflicts were not tracked, so these are a conservative lower bound.
Xu, Subramanian and Karthik 2026 (preprint): 42% of the conflicts between co-active agent pull requests were structural (modify/delete or add/add) and 58% content-based.

Ogenrwot and Businge 2026 (AgenticFlict, preprint; agent pull requests that were open or closed without merging, merged ones excluded): 27.67% conflicted with their base; the rate was about 9.9% at a median churn of 2 lines, nearly 30% at 25 lines, and levelled off for larger pull requests.

Pugachev 2025 (CodeCRDT, preprint, one author; Claude Sonnet 4.5, up to 5 agents on one shared CRDT document, 6 tasks, 50 runs per mode): parallel runs were 13.1% slower overall, from 21.1% faster to 39.4% slower by task, but produced more code and were faster per 1,000 characters in most tasks; a manual inspection of 60 of 600 runs gave a 5-10% semantic conflict rate with per-task figures of 20% and 80% that the paper does not reconcile.

Liu and others 2026 (STORM, preprint; the authors' own runs, Claude Sonnet 4.6, Commit0-Lite): every write declares the expected version of its file and is validated against the agent's full read snapshot; with at most 4 engineers (3.6 deployed on average) it reached 82.5% macro pass rate against 66.4% for one agent and 63.8% for isolated git worktrees; a rejected write gets the current file, a diff since its last read and its stale dependencies, plus a short reservation on the file so two agents cannot invalidate each other in a loop; no repeated runs are reported.

Liu and others 2026 (STORM, its own limits): it mediates the file editor tool but not writes made through bash; two agents editing different functions of one file trigger a false-positive rejection; heavily shared files such as __init__.py become serialization bottlenecks.

Liu and others 2026 (STORM): first-round overlap of file scopes rose from 21.7% of tasks at 4 engineers to 35.1% at 8 and correlated with rejected reviews (r = 0.28 overall, 0.78 within k=8); cost rose from $199 to $429 as the maximum went from 2 to 8 engineers, while wall-clock time stayed roughly constant.

Geng and Neubig 2026 (CAID, preprint; Claude Sonnet 4.5, isolated worktrees with a manager and tests per merge): on Commit0-Lite 59.1% against 53.1% for one agent, at 1583.2 s against 692.6 s and a cost of 8.1 against 1.9; worktrees beat instruction-only separation (59.1 against 56.1 %; on PaperBench 63.3 against 55.5 %); going from 4 to 8 engineers lowered the score. STORM's rerun of this worktree method (Sonnet 4.6, 4 engineers) scored 63.8% against 66.4% for one agent.

Yang, Nie and others 2026 (Co-Coder, preprint; all methods on gpt-5-mini, generation from a specification): partitioning by a static dependency graph lifted DevEval pass rate from 56.8% to 68.1% with a 1.81x speedup and 28% less cost, and one file per agent without that structure cost 44% more for a negligible gain; Claude Code with Agent Teams, run on gpt-5-mini through LiteLLM, had the lowest pass rate (16.3% on CodeProjectEval).
Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): long transactions also increase the likelihood of automatic aborts, to avoid deadlock or on failing validation in optimistic concurrency control.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): it is very undesirable to restart a long transaction that has done a significant amount of work; Pradel and others' snapshot validation restarts only for serious conflicts, where an object the transaction read was later changed by a transaction that finished during its read phase, so what it read was out of date; the longer the transaction the greater the risk of starvation; locking the whole database for a starving transaction is not acceptable for advanced applications.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey of Sun's NSE): developers work in private copies, and when conflicts are discovered they merge their changes instead of rolling back; a command, resync, tells a developer which objects others changed since the copy was taken.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): conflicts can be notified as soon as they occur or only when a conflicting transaction attempts to commit, with people resolving them, and humans might not really resolve conflicts, resulting in inconsistent data.

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): a problem that remains unsolved is the lack of performance metrics by which to evaluate these mechanisms, and the authors encountered only one empirical study (Yeh et al. 87).

Barghouti and Kaiser 1991 (survey): writers modifying two parts of one object with the intent of integrating them might need to look at each other's work, and insisting on serializable concurrency control in design environments might decrease concurrency or disallow desirable forms of cooperation.

Bancilhon, Kim and Korth 1985 (a formal model, no implementation or figure): a designer divides work into short transactions essentially for recovery purposes, and an abort induced by the system, due to a deadlock or system crash, aborts only the current short-duration transaction rather than the cooperating transaction.

Pu, Kaiser and Hutchinson 1988 (split-transactions, a design, no experiment): long transactions become concurrency bottlenecks because updated resources are retained for the duration of the transaction; a transaction can be split so that a finished part commits early when the read and write sets of the two parts allow a serial order.

Garcia-Molina and Salem 1987 (sagas; read from a poor OCR course copy; no measurement): a saga's compensating transaction undoes, from a semantic point of view, the actions of a step, but does not necessarily return the database to the state that existed before the step.

Perry, Siy and Votta 2001 (observational study of one subsystem of a large telephone switch over a 12-year period): 12.5% of all deltas were made to the same file by different developers within 24 hours of each other, and 3% of those deltas physically overlapped; the authors believe many more conflicts arise from semantic interference (a belief, not measured).

Perry, Siy and Votta 2001 (observational, a correlation): files with a high degree of parallel development had more defects, even accounting for lifetime, size and number of deltas; 55% of files never had more than one change open at a time and 0.6% had more than 6 parallel changes.

Figma 2019 (company blog, self-reported, no figures): one server process per document; a conflict happens only when two clients change the same property of the same object, and the document ends with the last value sent to the server; two edits of one text value keep one of them, never both.
Figma 2019 (company blog, self-reported): its multiplayer servers reject parent property updates that would cause a cycle in the document tree, an invariant across items checked at each write.

Google Docs engineers 2010 (Google Drive Blog, self-reported, no figures): locking paragraphs was rejected because an editor may find it did not actually acquire the lock; instead the server orders every change, transforms a late change against the revisions committed since the editor last synced, and each client never sends more than one pending change at a time; the posts hedge 'if OT is implemented correctly'.

Potvin and Levenberg 2016 (Google's single repository, self-reported, January 2015 figures): changes are made to the repository in a single, serial ordering, 16,000 a day by people and another 24,000 by automated systems; a change that breaks widely is automatically undone; long-lived branches with parallel development are exceedingly rare; no conflict or rollback rate is given.

Discord 2017 and 2023 (company blogs, self-reported): its Cassandra store resolved writes by last write wins per column, and an edit racing a delete left a row with only its key and text, which they detected and deleted at read; the later move to ScyllaDB was driven by hot partitions from concurrent reads, compaction backlogs and garbage-collection pauses, not by write contention.

Among the real-engine measurements read in lane w1, the longest units were FoundationDB's 5-second MVCC window (a design limit in its own paper, self-reported) and Tanabe and others' inserted delays of 0 to 10 ms (1 s ran out of memory); the 1977 Ries and Stonebraker simulation modelled transactions of 50 to 500 entities at an I/O rate of 100 msecs per entity and its authors concluded that in most cases 10 granules appear sufficient.

For harness builds the several-writers part of the rule is designed only, as read on 2026-11-19: conflicts per file are not logged, the merge script (research-tree/tools/merge.mjs), the modes table (research-tree/build/modes.json), the tier hook's Write/Edit branch and the build plan are named as new files, the build plan does not exist yet, writes through Bash or PowerShell are not seen, and only Write was seen refused.

Untested, rank 1 of the several-writers architecture: reshape shared places so writes commute or land at integration: each registry or list gets one entry per unit applied at landing, a number that must be the next free one is chosen at landing by one allocator, an ordered sequence becomes one step per unit (r57-0401's skeleton), units start in dependency order, and a writer-chosen unique name gets a duplicate check at landing; its value grows with the number of writers because it removes the hot place from the overlap; the share of each unit's diff on hot places and when in the unit it is written (M1) and whether entries applied at landing pass the check (M5) set its numbers.
